module_title: Weed Management and Orchard Floor Management

lessons.title: Common Weeds in Citrus Orchards
lessons.body: Weeds compete with citrus trees for water, nutrients, and sunlight, reducing yields by up to 30%. In African orchards, common grassy weeds include couch grass (Cynodon dactylon), which spreads via rhizomes and is drought-tolerant, and star grass (Cynodon nlemfuensis), often found in moist areas. Broadleaf weeds like blackjack (Bidens pilosa) and pigweed (Amaranthus spp.) grow quickly and host pests like aphids. Sedges such as purple nutsedge (Cyperus rotundus) thrive in wet, poorly drained soils and are hard to control because they produce underground tubers. Parasitic weeds like striga (Striga asiatica) attack citrus roots in some regions, stunting growth. Identify weeds early: couch grass has creeping stems and finger-like seed heads; blackjack has yellow flowers and sticky seeds; nutsedge has triangular stems and umbel-like flower clusters. Weeds are worst in young orchards where tree canopies don't shade the ground. In mature orchards, shade suppresses many weeds, but aggressive species still emerge. Keep records of which weeds appear and whereâthis guides your control strategy. For example, if you see nutsedge, you know the soil is too wet and you may need to improve drainage. Regular scouting every 2 weeks helps you act before weeds seed. A single blackjack plant can produce 3,000 seeds, so never let them flower. In Africa, many farmers use local knowledge: some weeds like amaranth are edible and can be harvested, but be careful not to let them go to seed. Knowing your weeds saves money on herbicides and labor. Start by walking your orchard weekly and noting the top three weeds. That's your first step toward effective management.

lessons.title: Mechanical and Manual Weed Control
lessons.body: Mechanical and manual methods are the backbone of weed control in African citrus orchards, especially where herbicides are expensive or unavailable. Hand hoeing is common but labor-intensive: one worker can clear about 0.1 hectare per day. Use a sharp hoe to cut weeds at the soil surface, avoiding deep digging that damages citrus feeder roots. For larger areas, a slasher or machete can knock down tall weeds, but you must repeat every 4-6 weeks during the rainy season. Mowers (brush cutters) are faster: a petrol-powered brush cutter can clear 0.5 hectare per day, but keep the blade 5 cm above the soil to avoid root injury. In row middles, a tractor-mounted rotary mower can cover 2 hectares per day, but avoid mowing close to tree trunks. Cultivation with a disc harrow or tine cultivator is effective in dry season, but in wet soils it can compact the soil and spread rhizomatous weeds like couch grass. For small orchards, hand pulling is best for weeds near the trunk, especially vines that climb trees. Timing is critical: control weeds before they flower and set seed. In Africa, many farmers use the 'slash and mulch' method: cut weeds with a slasher, then leave the cuttings as mulch around trees. This suppresses new weeds and adds organic matter. However, don't let cuttings touch the trunkâthey can harbor pests. Avoid deep tillage in the root zone (within 1 meter of the trunk) because citrus roots are shallow. Repeated shallow hoeing (2-3 cm deep) is safer. Mulching with cut weeds can also reduce germination of new weeds. Remember that mechanical control is most effective when combined with other methods. For example, after hoeing, apply a thick mulch to slow regrowth. Always clean tools between blocks to prevent spreading weed seeds or diseases.

lessons.title: Herbicide Selection and Application
lessons.body: Herbicides can be a cost-effective tool for weed control in citrus, but choose carefully to avoid tree damage. Pre-emergent herbicides like simazine, diuron, and oxyfluorfen are applied to bare soil before weeds emerge. They form a chemical barrier that kills germinating weed seeds. Apply them to a weed-free soil surface in early spring or after rains, at rates of 2-4 kg active ingredient per hectare. Do not apply pre-emergents if you plan to plant cover crops. Post-emergent herbicides like glyphosate (Roundup) and glufosinate (Basta) kill existing weeds. Glyphosate is systemic and kills perennial weeds like couch grass, but it is non-selectiveâany spray that hits citrus leaves will damage the tree. Use a shielded sprayer or direct the nozzle at the base of weeds, keeping spray off the trunk and foliage. For young trees, wrap the trunk with a protective guard. Apply glyphosate at 1-2% solution (10-20 ml per liter of water) when weeds are actively growing and not drought-stressed. Add a surfactant (e.g., 0.5% non-ionic) to improve coverage. In Africa, many farmers use knapsack sprayers (15-20 L capacity). Calibrate your sprayer: mark a 100 mÂ² area, spray with water, and measure how much you used. Then mix herbicide accordingly. Always wear protective clothing: gloves, goggles, long sleeves, and boots. Avoid spraying on windy days (over 10 km/h) to prevent drift. Do not spray when rain is expected within 6 hours. Rotate herbicides with different modes of action to prevent resistanceâfor example, alternate glyphosate with glufosinate. Keep records of what you spray, when, and where. Store herbicides in a locked cabinet away from children and food. Never mix more than you need, and triple-rinse empty containers before disposal. Herbicides are poisonsâuse them responsibly.

lessons.title: Mulching for Weed Suppression
lessons.body: Mulching is one of the best ways to suppress weeds, conserve moisture, and improve soil health in citrus orchards. Organic mulches like straw, dry grass, maize stover, and wood chips are spread 5-10 cm thick around the tree, starting 10 cm away from the trunk (to prevent rot) and extending to the drip line. A 1-hectare orchard needs about 20-30 tonnes of mulch for a 5 cm layer. In Africa, farmers often use locally available materials: banana leaves, coffee husks, rice hulls, or even shredded paper. Avoid using fresh grass clippings, which can heat up and damage roots, or mulches that contain weed seeds (e.g., hay with mature seeds). Black plastic mulch (UV-stabilized) is effective for weed control and warms the soil, but it is costly and degrades after 2-3 years. It is best for high-value young trees. Biodegradable plastic mulches (e.g., starch-based) are becoming available. Apply mulch after clearing existing weeds and irrigating. Reapply annually as it decomposes. Mulch reduces weed germination by blocking light, and it also moderates soil temperature, reduces evaporation, and adds organic matter as it breaks down. However, mulch can attract termites and rodentsâmonitor and control if needed. In wet areas, mulch may increase disease pressure, so keep it away from the trunk. For weed suppression, a 7-10 cm layer of coarse wood chips works best. Combine mulch with hand weeding for best results. Mulching also improves fruit quality by keeping soil moisture consistent. In dry regions like the Sahel, mulching is essential for young tree survival. Start mulching at planting and maintain a continuous layer. It's a long-term investment that pays off in healthier trees and fewer weeds.

lessons.title: Cover Cropping for Weed Management
lessons.body: Cover crops are plants grown between orchard rows to suppress weeds, improve soil, and support beneficial insects. In African citrus orchards, good cover crops include legumes like cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), lablab (Lablab purpureus), and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan), which fix nitrogen and grow quickly. Grasses like rye (Secale cereale) and sorghum-sudan hybrids produce lots of biomass and smother weeds. Legumes like clover (Trifolium spp.) are low-growing and can be mowed. Choose cover crops that are not invasive and are suited to your climate. In dry areas, use drought-tolerant species like cowpea or lablab. In wet areas, use vigorous growers like sorghum-sudan. Plant cover crops in the rainy season when soil is moist. Broadcast seed at 20-50 kg per hectare for legumes, or 50-100 kg for grasses. Rake lightly to cover seed, or use a roller. Irrigate if no rain within 3 days. Once established, cover crops compete with weeds for light, water, and nutrients. Mow or roll them before they set seed to prevent them becoming weeds. You can also chop and drop: cut the cover crop and leave residue as mulch. This adds organic matter and suppresses weeds. Terminate cover crops before they compete with citrus for waterâusually at flowering. In young orchards, keep cover crops at least 1 meter from tree trunks to avoid competition. Cover crops can also host pests like aphids, so monitor and manage. Some farmers use living mulches like sweet potato or creeping peanut, which spread along the ground. Cover cropping reduces herbicide use and improves soil health. It's a key part of integrated weed management. Start with a small area to see what works, then expand.

lessons.title: Integrated Weed Management Plans
lessons.body: Integrated Weed Management (IWM) combines multiple methods to control weeds effectively with minimal chemicals. Start by scouting your orchard every 2 weeks to identify weeds and their growth stages. Map problem areasâfor example, wet spots where nutsedge thrives. Set an action threshold: for young trees, control weeds when they reach 15 cm tall; for mature trees, when they compete for water or nutrients. Combine cultural, mechanical, biological, and chemical methods. Cultural: maintain healthy trees with proper spacing (5-6 m between trees) so canopies shade the ground. Apply mulch (5-10 cm) around trees. Plant cover crops in row middles during rainy season. Mechanical: hoe or mow before weeds seed. Use a brush cutter for large areas. Hand pull weeds near trunks. Chemical: use pre-emergent herbicides in early spring, and spot-spray post-emergent herbicides only where needed. Rotate herbicides to prevent resistance. Biological: encourage natural enemies of weeds, such as geese (they eat grass) or goats (but they may damage treesâuse fencing). In Africa, some farmers use chickens to scratch and eat weed seeds. Create a yearly plan: in dry season, focus on mulching and hand weeding; in rainy season, use cover crops and mowing. Keep records: date, weed species, method used, cost, and effectiveness. Review and adjust. For example, if couch grass persists, increase mulch thickness or use glyphosate spot sprays. Train workers on proper herbicide application and safety. Budget for IWM: labor is often the biggest cost, but it can be reduced by 30% with mulching and cover crops. IWM is not about eliminating all weedsâsome weeds support beneficial insects. Aim to keep weeds below economic threshold. A good IWM plan saves money, protects the environment, and improves tree health. Start small, monitor, and adapt.

quiz.q: Which weed is a sedge that thrives in wet, poorly drained soils?
quiz.explanation: Purple nutsedge (Cyperus rotundus) is a sedge that prefers wet soils and produces underground tubers.

quiz.q: What is a key characteristic of couch grass?
quiz.explanation: Couch grass spreads through rhizomes, making it difficult to control.

quiz.q: Why is it important to identify weeds early in citrus orchards?
options: A) To know which ones are edible
B) To prevent them from producing seeds
C) To decide on the best herbicide
quiz.explanation: Early identification allows control before weeds set seed, reducing future infestations.

quiz.q: Which weed can produce up to 3,000 seeds per plant?
quiz.explanation: Blackjack (Bidens pilosa) is a prolific seed producer, with up to 3,000 seeds per plant.

quiz.q: What is a common method for manual weed control near citrus trunks?
quiz.explanation: Hand pulling is safe near trunks because it avoids root damage and herbicide injury.

quiz.q: How deep should you hoe to avoid damaging citrus feeder roots?
quiz.explanation: Shallow hoeing (2-3 cm) prevents damage to shallow citrus roots.

quiz.q: What is the 'slash and mulch' method?
options: A) Cutting weeds and leaving them as mulch
quiz.explanation: Slash and mulch involves cutting weeds and leaving the cuttings to suppress new growth and add organic matter.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid deep tillage within 1 meter of the tree trunk?
options: B) It damages shallow citrus roots
quiz.explanation: Citrus roots are shallow; deep tillage can cut and damage them.

quiz.q: Which pre-emergent herbicide is commonly used in citrus?
quiz.explanation: Simazine is a pre-emergent herbicide that controls germinating weed seeds.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration for glyphosate application?
quiz.explanation: A 1-2% solution (10-20 ml per liter) is effective for most weeds.

quiz.q: Why should you add a surfactant to glyphosate?
options: B) To improve coverage on leaves
quiz.explanation: Surfactants help the herbicide spread and stick to weed leaves for better absorption.

quiz.q: What is a key safety practice when applying herbicides?
quiz.explanation: Protective clothing prevents skin contact and inhalation of toxic chemicals.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be for effective weed suppression?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer blocks light and suppresses weed germination.

quiz.q: Why should mulch be kept 10 cm away from the tree trunk?
options: A) To prevent rot and pest damage
quiz.explanation: Mulch against the trunk can cause bark rot and attract pests like termites.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT recommended as mulch?
quiz.explanation: Fresh grass clippings heat up and can damage roots; they should be dried first.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of black plastic mulch?
quiz.explanation: Black plastic mulch warms the soil and suppresses weeds, but it is costly and non-biodegradable.

quiz.q: Which cover crop is a legume that fixes nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is a legume that fixes nitrogen and suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: When should cover crops be terminated?
options: C) At the end of the dry season
D) When they are 1 meter tall
quiz.explanation: Terminating before flowering prevents cover crops from becoming weeds.

quiz.q: What is a potential disadvantage of cover crops?
options: A) They compete with citrus for water
quiz.explanation: Cover crops can compete with citrus for water and nutrients, especially in dry periods.

quiz.q: How far should cover crops be kept from young tree trunks?
quiz.explanation: Keeping cover crops 1 meter from trunks reduces competition for water and nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the first step in an Integrated Weed Management plan?
quiz.explanation: Scouting identifies weed species and problem areas, guiding management decisions.

quiz.q: What is an action threshold for weed control in young citrus orchards?
quiz.explanation: Controlling weeds when they reach 15 cm prevents competition and seed production.

quiz.q: Which method is NOT part of Integrated Weed Management?
quiz.explanation: Deep tillage is not recommended as it damages citrus roots and can spread weeds.

quiz.q: How can chickens help in weed management?
quiz.explanation: Chickens scratch the soil and eat weed seeds, reducing weed populations.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of rotating herbicides?
quiz.explanation: Rotating herbicides with different modes of action prevents weeds from developing resistance.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records in an IWM plan?
options: A) To track costs and effectiveness
B) To sell to other farmers
quiz.explanation: Records help monitor what works, adjust methods, and budget for future seasons.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using glyphosate?
options: A) Spraying on a calm day
B) Getting spray on citrus leaves
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate is non-selective and will damage citrus foliage if it contacts it.

quiz.q: How often should you scout for weeds in a citrus orchard?
quiz.explanation: Regular scouting every 2 weeks helps catch weeds before they spread or seed.

quiz.q: What is a living mulch?
options: A) A cover crop that grows low and spreads
quiz.explanation: Living mulches like sweet potato or creeping peanut grow along the ground and suppress weeds.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of Integrated Weed Management?
options: B) To keep weeds below economic threshold
quiz.explanation: IWM aims to manage weeds at levels that don't cause economic loss, not to eradicate them.
